lead: An autopilot closes the control loop automatically. Sensors measure the aircraft's actual attitude, rate or path. A computer compares that with the commanded value and sends a correction. Servos move the surfaces or the throttles. The pilot selects a mode and a target; the machine holds it. This frees attention for navigation and monitoring, and it is the basis of every automatic flight control system (AFCS), from a light aircraft wing leveller to an airliner autoland.
prereq: You need: the powered actuators of Chapter 1.3 and the computer-driven control laws of Chapter 1.5, because the autopilot commands those actuators and uses those computers.

blocks.text: An automatic flight control system (AFCS) is a closed loop. The pilot or a navigation receiver gives a command. Sensors measure the actual aircraft state. A computer subtracts actual from commanded to get an error, shapes a correction, and sends it to a servo. The servo moves a control surface or a thrust lever. The aircraft responds, the sensors see the new state, and the loop repeats.

The sensors are gyros for attitude and rate, an inertial measurement unit (IMU) for acceleration and rate, air data for airspeed and altitude, and a radio altimeter for height above the ground during approach. The computer is usually a flight control computer with redundancy. The servo is an electro-hydraulic or electro-mechanical actuator. The mode selector tells the computer what to hold; the disconnect button removes servo power and returns control to the pilot.

The inner loop is fast and holds attitude or rate: pitch rate, roll rate and yaw damping. The outer loop is slower and holds a path: altitude, heading, speed or a radio navigation course. The outer loop sends its target to the inner loop, as a heading select mode asks the roll channel for a bank angle.
δ<sub>a</sub> = K<sub>p</sub> e − K<sub>r</sub> p (roll); δ<sub>e</sub> = K<sub>p</sub> e − K<sub>r</sub> q (pitch)
blocks.where: For the roll channel: δ<sub>a</sub> is the aileron command in degrees; p is the roll rate in degrees per second, positive right. For the pitch channel: δ<sub>e</sub> is the elevator command in degrees, positive nose-up; q is the pitch rate in degrees per second, positive nose-up. e is the error between commanded and actual attitude in degrees. K<sub>p</sub> is the proportional gain in degrees per degree. K<sub>r</sub> is the rate gain in degrees per degree per second; it has units of seconds. The minus sign damps the motion.

blocks.text: Pitch hold and roll hold keep the current attitude. Altitude hold uses the outer loop to command small pitch changes. Heading select commands a bank angle until the heading error is zero. VOR/LOC and glide-slope coupling let the autopilot follow a radio beam: localizer for lateral, glide slope for vertical. Autoland adds redundant sensors, computers and servos, and is classified as Category I, II or III by decision height and runway visual range.

Low-speed protection and upset protection watch for stall or unusual attitude and push the aircraft back to a safe state. Disengagement logic removes the autopilot when the pilot presses the disconnect button, when a sensor fails, or when the servo is forced against a limit. Some systems give an aural warning before disconnect.

Rate feedback exists because proportional control alone overshoots. If the aircraft is rolling toward the target, the proportional term still commands a large correction. The rate term subtracts a command proportional to how fast the aircraft is already moving. The result is a smaller command near the target and a smooth stop.

On a Cessna 172R, a simple single-axis wing leveller uses one servo on the ailerons and a turn coordinator as its rate sensor. The turn coordinator is primarily a rate-of-turn instrument; its canted gyro also responds to roll rate, and the wing leveller uses that roll-rate signal. It does not measure bank angle. If a wing drops, the servo moves the ailerons to level the wings. It cannot hold altitude or fly a heading by itself; the pilot still controls pitch and power.
Active control technology goes further, using the same surfaces for load alleviation and stability augmentation; see Chapter 1.7.

The auto-throttle system (ATS) moves the thrust levers. It does not move the elevator. In speed hold it compares actual speed with the selected speed and moves the levers to reduce the error. In Mach hold it does the same with Mach number. Take-off/go-around (TOGA) moves the levers to the take-off or go-around thrust limit.

Auto-throttle helps in gusty air because the thrust changes quickly while the pilot keeps a steady attitude. On approach it holds speed while the autopilot follows the glide slope, so the pilot monitors rather than chases the throttles. It is not a pitch control. If speed is low, the auto-throttle adds thrust; the autopilot continues to hold the selected path with pitch. A descent to regain speed belongs only to a speed-on-pitch mode, not the usual auto-throttle split.

The same loop structure applies: error, gain, actuator. A speed error of 5 kt might produce a small lever movement; a large error produces a larger movement. Rate of change of speed can be fed back to damp the response, just as rate feedback damps the roll channel.

figure.caption: Automatic flight control splits into a fast inner attitude loop, a slower outer path loop, and the auto-throttle that sets thrust. Notice that rate damping and yaw damping sit in the inner loop.

examples.question: A roll channel uses 3° of aileron per degree of roll error and 0.8° of aileron per degree per second of roll rate, with the rate term subtracted. At one instant the aircraft is 4° left of the commanded bank and rolling right at 2°/s. Find the aileron command and the share removed by rate feedback.
steps: Set e = +4° for the 4° left bank error, because the correction needed is to the right. Set p = +2°/s for the right roll rate. A positive result means right aileron.
Proportional command = K<sub>p</sub> × e = 3 × 4 = 12° of aileron.
Rate share = K<sub>r</sub> × p = 0.8 × 2 = 1.6° of aileron.
Aileron command δ = K<sub>p</sub> e − K<sub>r</sub> p = 12 − 1.6 = 10.4° of right aileron.
Rate share as a percentage of the proportional command = 1.6 ÷ 12 × 100 = 13.3 %. The rate term removes about 13 % of the proportional command and damps the roll.
examples.answer: The aileron command is 10.4° of right aileron; rate feedback removes 1.6°, about 13.3 % of the 12° proportional command.
examples.check:
Kp = 3.0
Kr = 0.8
e = 4.0
p = 2.0
delta = Kp * e - Kr * p
rate_share = Kr * p
percent = rate_share / (Kp * e) * 100
print(f"{delta:.1f}")
print(f"{rate_share:.1f}")
print(f"{percent:.1f}")

traps: The auto-throttle moves thrust levers only; it never commands pitch. Saying it controls altitude is wrong unless the autopilot pitch channel is also engaged.
An autopilot without servos is only a computer. The servo is the part that moves the surface or lever.

The rate term is subtracted algebraically when p is positive in the direction of the error; if the aircraft is rolling away from the target, p has the opposite sign and the rate term adds to the correction. Adding rate feedback with the wrong sign makes the response less damped and increases overshoot.
A single-axis wing leveller holds wings level; it does not hold altitude or heading by itself.
Autoland Category I, II or III depends on decision height and runway visual range, not on the number of autopilot channels alone.

quiz.q: What does the inner loop of an AFCS hold, and what does the outer loop hold?
quiz.a: Inner loop holds attitude or rate: pitch, roll and yaw damping. Outer loop holds a path such as altitude, heading, speed or a navigation course.

quiz.q: Why is the rate term subtracted from the proportional term?
quiz.a: It opposes the existing motion, reducing the command near the target and preventing overshoot or oscillation.

quiz.q: A roll channel has K<sub>p</sub> = 2.5° per degree and K<sub>r</sub> = 0.6° per degree per second. The aircraft is 6° from the commanded bank and rolling at 3°/s in the same sense as the error. Find the aileron command and the rate share.
quiz.a: δ = 2.5 × 6 − 0.6 × 3 = 15 − 1.8 = 13.2°. Rate share = 1.8°, about 12 % of the proportional 15°.

quiz.q: What happens if the roll-rate sensor fails to zero while the autopilot stays engaged?
quiz.a: The rate term disappears. The roll channel becomes proportional only, so it overshoots and may oscillate. A good system detects the failure and disconnects or reduces gain.

quiz.q: What does the auto-throttle move, and name two of its modes.
quiz.a: It moves the thrust levers. Speed hold and Mach hold are two modes; TOGA is another.

quiz.q: What is the sensor and actuator in the Cessna 172R wing leveller, and what does the sensor supply?
quiz.a: The sensor is a turn coordinator; it supplies a rate signal, and the wing leveller uses its roll-rate response. It does not measure bank angle. The actuator is one servo on the ailerons.

quiz.q: Why does autoland need more than a normal autopilot?
quiz.a: It needs redundant sensors, computers and servos, automatic landing guidance, and fail-operational behaviour so a single failure does not lose the approach. It must also meet decision-height and runway-visual-range limits for its category.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, AFCS work connects to software assurance under RTCA DO-178C, data buses such as ARINC 429 and ARINC 664, and handling-qualities standards. Newer curricula discuss envelope protection, autonomous landing and urban air mobility. Search for autopilot inner loop outer loop, autoland category, and auto-throttle TOGA to go further.
